subsubtopic: FUTURE OF HAWKER SIDDELEY CAR WORKS AT TRENTON, N. S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my frustration at the lack of action being taken by the Government of Canada and the Province of Nova Scotia in regard to the continued operation of the Hawker Siddeley Trenton Car Works in Pictou County, Nova Scotia.
Since the company gave notice some weeks ago, the Government of Nova Scotia and the federal Government came together to try to find a solution to this very difficult problem. Unfortunately, since that time meetings have taken place but indeed there has been no action. In fact the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) indicated to the House that a solution would have been found within weeks. Unfortunately, there is no solution.
All we are receiving from the national Government as well as the provincial Government is more delays. I suggest that these delays are very harmful to the people of that particular community. It is frustrating to the workers at the Hawker Siddeley plant in Trenton, Nova Scotia. Equally, the uncertainty of a lack of a decisive decision with regard to the future of that operation is causing havoc throughout Pictou County.
I call upon the Government to stand up and be counted, and to make a decisive, positive decision on behalf of the workers and community in that area.

subsubtopic: SALES OF BOTTLED WATER-RESULTS OF TESTS- ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Consumers' Association reports that sales of bottled water have doubled since 1982. The average Canadian now drinks four litres a year. In Quebec the consumption is twice a much as the average. At the same time, using standards set by the United States Environmental Protection Agency, the Consumers' Association tested 15 brands of commercial bottled spring water for 79 substances and concluded that bottled water is not purer or safer to drink than tap water.
The Consumers' Association's tests showed that all the brands tested contained dissolved metals, inorganic chemicals and other suspended particles often at higher levels than tap water in seven Canadian cities. What lesson can we draw from all this?
It is becoming more obvious every day that what we do in our environment eventually affects water, even spring water. Everything in the environment is connected to everything else. What we do above the ground ultimately affects ground water, even if it is hundreds of metres below the surface. The first step we must take to reverse this trend is to abandon the dangerous mindset, the "out of sight-out of mind" attitude.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MEDICINE HAT TIGERS-MEMORIAL HOCKEY CUP CHAMPIONS
TRIBUTE TO MEDICINE HAT TIGERS-MEMORIAL HOCKEY CUP CHAMPIONS
speechtext:

subsubtopic: RADON GAS-HIGH LEVELS IN SOUTHERN SASKATCHEWAN HOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, studies conducted in the past several years show that Saskatchewan has the highest levels of radon gas in the country. According to news reports 27 per cent of homes surveyed in southern Saskatchewan have radon levels four times the normal level. This means that occupants of those homes are exposed to radiation equivalent to more than 200 chest X-rays a year. The same surveys show Regina and Winnipeg as the cities with the highest radon levels in the country.
Most of these surveys were done during the summer months. A survey during winter would show even higher levels. These results of high radon gas levels are of grave concern to us and reveal an urgent need for action.
What is needed are more surveys, especially during winter months. The results of these surveys should be made public immediately rather than years later. Home owners should also be given an opportunity to monitor radon levels in their homes. More public information is also needed. Home builders, local building and health authorities, as well as individual home owners, have got to know what they can do to reduce the radon gas to acceptable levels.
May 20, 1987

I urge the federal Government to provide leadership that will make the homes in the areas of high radon gas emissions safe homes in which to live.

subsubtopic: ATTACK BY PRESIDENT ON BRITISH COLUMBIA PREMIER AS "NEW CANADIAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked and disappointed this past weekend to hear comments made by Shirley Carr, President of the Canadian Labour Congress. In a speech praising the New Democratic Party she launched an attack against the Premier of British Columbia, Mr. Bill Vander Zalm. What was most troubling was her comment that Mr. Vander Zalm as "a new Canadian" should remember who helped liberate his country during World War II and that he had no right to bring his fascist ideas to this country.
I reject any distinction being made between native born and new Canadians. She should remember that, with the exception of our native groups, we were all new Canadians. As a nation we have never placed any limitation on a person's right to speak based on his country of origin, nor should we.
This kind of intolerance is unacceptable, un-Canadian, and I am sure is repudiated by the membership of the Canadian Labour Congress.

subsubtopic: CANCELLATION OF EXPANSION PROJECT AT WESTMORLAND INSTITUTION IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House an action by the Government which my constituents find totally unacceptable.
We have learned through access to information that the Government has cancelled an $18 million upgrading and expansion project at Westmorland Institution in southeast New Brunswick. While the Government cancelled Westmorland, and other important projects across Canada, it approved the construction of a $68 million penitentiary in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding, a facility which most everyone agrees is not needed.

The Government's decision to build a new institution in the Prime Minister's riding, at the expense of other regions, is entirely unacceptable, especially when you consider that the unemployment rate in my own riding is 17.5 per cent, which is outrageous.
How do we explain this to the people of New Brunswick? We can only say the Government has decided to forget they exist!

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CONSTRUCTION OF ALUMINUM PLANT AT LATERRIERE IN JONQUIERE CONSTITUENCY
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, it sounds like good news. Unfortunately, with the new plant and the new technology that will be used, Jonquiere will suffer a net loss of nearly 750 jobs. Add to that the loss in taxes and the good news becomes rather alarming for the community of Jonquiere.

Alcan cannot go on investing all around Jonquiere while abandoning a community that has served it so well. We need more than the 4 or 5 million invested in SOCCRENT for our community. The company's directors are in the big league. They can afford to attract other investment to our region to diversify the local economy and maintain job levels in Jonquiere.
The community of Jonquiere is very worried, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG PERSONS OVER 45 YEARS OF AGE-COMMITTEE'S STUDY OF AGE DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unemployment is not only a regional problem, it is also an age problem. Unemployed Canadians 45 years of age and over are more likely to suffer permanent long-term unemployment than any other age group.
This is only one example, Mr. Speaker, of actual age discrimination in Canada, in spite of federal and provincial legislation against such discrimination.
For that reason the Human Rights Committee of this House will begin a study on age discrimination today, and we hope to visit western Canada next week to receive testimony from that region. For that, we need the approval of the House. I hope that the Opposition will not thwart the opportunity for western Canada to participate fully in this vital study.

He is now getting involved in this matter as he should have been all along. If he is serious about this is he prepared to take positive measures to ensure that other Canadian companies can bid for Dome without prohibitive lawsuits from Amoco?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROPOSED PURCHASE OF DOME PETROLEUM BY AMOCO CANADA-POSSIBILITY OF OTHER BIDS

POSSIBILITY OF CERTAIN CANADIAN COMPANIES OFFERING TO BUY DOME-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
I have a supplementary for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
A number of Canadian companies including TransCanada PipeLines, Imperial Oil, Husky and Petro-Canada may be making a bid to purchase Dome. Is the Minister prepared to consider such a bid and is he prepared to help these companies? We want a Canadian solution. Does the Minister also want a Canadian solution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CERTAIN CANADIAN COMPANIES OFFERING TO BUY DOME-GOVERNMENT POSITION

As for the future of such proposals, it is entirely up to the people in charge of Dome to decide whether they like them or not.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In September of 1986 the Prime Minister said we had a drug epidemic in Canada. I did not agree with him at that time but shortly thereafter the principal of a Mississauga high school told me that 50 per cent of the students I spoke to that day were using drugs.
May 20, 1987

I know $50 billion from the sale of illegal drugs is laundered each year in North America. I have since found out there are many drug-related gangland slayings around the city of Toronto. As a former member of the RCMP and on behalf of many concerned parents I would ask when is the Government going to do something about this abhorrent situation, and what is it going to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is essential that all Members understand the importance of this issue, the importance the Prime Minister placed on it, and the public profile he gave to it. Since that statement was made I and other Members of the House have been confronted on this issue by parents and people who work with youth. There has been very close co-operation between the federal Government, the provinces, and those agencies working on drug and alcohol addiction. We believe that is a good plan. We intend to unveil it across the country next week.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. I am certain he would agree that the union and management at the Saint John Shipyard ought to be congratulated for their good and efficient work on the first phase of the frigate program. Can he indicate to the House, and particularly to the people of Saint John, whether or not the Government is still committed to the second phase of that program whereby six additional frigates will be built in Canada by Canadians, and that the decision will be made before October, 1987?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly join with my hon. friend in congratulating the workers at Saint John Shipyard on the fine work they are doing. I have heard directly from them, my colleague the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines, the Premier of New Brunswick, as well as the Mayor of Saint John. They all made the case that the Saint John Shipyard is capable of doing superb work.
We will be announcing the architecture of the new Canadian Navy in the defence White Paper which will be coming out very shortly. My hon. friend will have his answer at that time.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister said the western diversification initiative would be announced at the earliest possible moment. I have here a leaked letter from the Minister of DRIE which he was planning to send out to some business people in western Canada to start consultation, with 30 key business leaders. The letter has not yet been sent out, but there are supposed to be consultations between April 22 and June 12 according to another leaked document I have.
Since this letter has not yet gone out and the consultations have not yet started I want to know why the unacceptable delay? Why has this important project been stalled? Does he not know we have very serious economic problems in western Canada? Why are you pushing us around like that? We want action now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would agree that it is not customary for a cabinet Minister to comment on a so-called leaked letter that was planned to be sent out by anyone.
Maybe the Government should develop the custom of at least answering the questions put by the Opposition.
Give us a sensible question.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a copy of a western diversification report or questionnaire used by public servants when they conducted a survey of western Canadian businesses. I understand a questionnaire of several pages is now being completed with about 24 different sector groups.
Perhaps the Deputy Prime Minister could answer the first question and at the same time tell us why, during this round of consultations, the Government is planning to consult only with the business community in western Canada? Why not consult

May 20, 1987
Oral Questions
as well with provincial Governments, municipalities, the farm sector, trade unions and others across the west? Why only with the business community at this stage?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:

As a matter of fact, we are criticized every day from across the way for consulting too much with provincial Governments. Some have suggested we are giving away too much federal power to the provinces. The fact is that consultations have gone on.
As to responding to questions, if the Hon. Member put a thoughtful question I would certainly answer it. Hypothetical questions are not the kind of questions that I or any Minister, or even the Member I am sure, would like to answer.

subsubtopic: TEACHING OF FRENCH IN DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE-BIDDING OFFERS-ABSENCE OF PARTICIPATION BY QUEBEC FIRMS

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PROVIDE JOBS AT LEVIS-LAUZON SHIPYARDS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PROVIDE JOBS AT LEVIS-LAUZON SHIPYARDS
speechtext:
Another question, Mr. Speaker, again related to regional development. The Minister responsible for this Department being absent, perhaps I might direct my question to the Prime Minister because it concerns the important Levis-Lauzon region. I learned over the weekend that there are only 400 workers left
at the Lauzon shipyards, and that half of them are going to be laid off very soon. If we go back a few years to early September 1984 when this Government came into office, 1,500 Levis-Lauzon region workers had jobs at the shipyards.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister what the Government is waiting for to award a contract and begin work on the Caribou II ferry, which might provide employment for these Levis-Lauzon workers?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PROVIDE JOBS AT LEVIS-LAUZON SHIPYARDS
speechtext: Interestingly enough, Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate in the Levis-Lauzon region is now lower than it was on September 17, 1984, much lower. I should think my friend would agree with me that this is due mainly to federal contract award initiatives in the greater Quebec City metropolitan area, and particularly in that region. The federal Government will be taking action in a number of cases precisely to lower even more the unacceptably high unemployment rate in that region and maintain wide-ranging activities on a regional basis. We will be making statements to that effect in the not too distant future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. It concerns his statement in the House yesterday when he said, in response to a question by the Hon. Member for Papineau with respect to VIA Rail:
We will continue with new maintenance facilities, including facilities in
Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Halifax.
Does this statement mean that the postponement of those new facilities in Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Halifax has ended and the building of these facilities will commence? If so, when?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statement means exactly what it says, that because of the additional funding which we are now providing for VIA Rail, VIA Rail will be able to go forward with its plans to construct maintenance facilities in Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Halifax. It will have to produce a plan for my approval and it will have to be part of its fiscal and annual plan. All those procedures will have to be followed.
It means that we are giving VIA the financial wherewithal to go forward with these maintenance facilities, including the completion of the construction of the facilities at Toronto and Montreal.
May 20, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate the Minister giving us a bit more detail about the timeframe he envisages for beginning these projects because it is certainly something that would be economically significant for western Canada as well as Atlantic Canada.
Perhaps the Minister could elaborate on that and, while doing so, tell us whether the Government intends to give any instruction to VIA with respect to its plans to shorten its train this summer, at the very time when there is increased demand for passenger rail service in Canada? We are told that VIA is planning to have a 14-car train instead of its usual 21-car train. Will the Government do anything about that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot give any more details in connection with the construction of maintenance facilities until I have met with VIA Rail and received its latest plans and schedule. The additional funding we are providing is over a five-year period and VIA will have to bring forward a plan which indicates where, when, and how they will proceed.
With respect to the second part of the Hon. Member's question, it is not that VIA Rail plans to shorten its trains this summer; it plans not to lengthen them. It will not add cars to its train services. What I am saying is 100 per cent accurate: it is not shortening the trains, it will simply not lengthen them.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT EMBASSY BE REOPENED IN BEIRUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question which is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerns the Middle East. In 1985 the Government designated May 6 as Canada-Lebanon Day. During recent celebrations with the Lebanese community here in Ottawa, strong pleas were made for the Government to reopen its embassy in Beirut.
We all recognize the terrible tragedies that are still occurring in Beirut and in the Middle East. However, is the Government giving any consideration to reopening our embassy in Beirut in order to allow Canadians of Lebanese origin more easily and effectively to reunite their families here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT EMBASSY BE REOPENED IN BEIRUT

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for that question and for the constant interest that he and the Minister of Public Works and others in the House have shown in the matter of our situation in Lebanon. We took the decision to close our embassy there because we thought it was not safe to maintain it open. Circumstances in Lebanon have not changed since that decision was taken.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, in light of the Minister's response, would it be possible for the Government to consider setting up an immigration liaison operation with the British Embassy or another embassy in Beirut in order to make it easier for Lebanese people who want to come to Canada to join Canadians of Lebanese origin?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am naturally prepared to consider that. I would not want my remarks to be taken as any more commitment than to consider that proposal. However, we will look at that as a means to supplement the service that we now try to extend to a city where it is not possible for us to maintain an embassy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. He knows that northern Ontario has faced a very difficult time in the last couple of years with losses in the steel, forestry, and the mining industries. Will he explain why the Government is making the situation worse by transferring and cutting out hundreds of federal government jobs which not only take away wages in northern Ontario but take away services? Why has the Province of Ontario been able to transfer 1,200 jobs, with whole departments of government, into northern Ontario while the federal Government is transferring jobs out?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated in the House before, the northern Ontario initiative is in its final stages of preparation. I have indicated on previous occasions that, in close co-operation with the Solicitor General, a program will be announced very soon which I believe will do much to establish a firm economic foundation for northern Ontario, which is something that had been sadly lacking during the previous administration.

Mr. Speaker, will the Deputy Prime Minister assure us that the Government will change its policies in this recovery program because we have lost some 450 jobs as a result of the Canada-U.S. export tax deal, lost hundreds of jobs in the steel industry at the tube mill at Sault Ste. Marie because of the energy policy of the Government, and our service industry has been hurt because of the cut-backs in the Small Craft Harbours Program? Will the Minister tell us today the date of the recovery program so that northern Ontario can begin to improve rather than decline as it has in the last two and one-half years?

May 20, 1987
Oral Questions

Southern Ontario.

I agree that a number of them have been created in southern Ontario. The fact is that we recognize that there is this regional imbalance to which the Prime Minister has referred on many occasions. We are addressing that.

Like softwood lumber.

speechtext: -to ensure that we would prevent the kinds of actions as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry suggested with regard to the softwood lumber issue. We need in place an equitable and workable dispute resolving mechanism, together with all the other components of an agreement which would enhance and secure our trading relationship with the United States. That would be in the best interests of northern Ontario and that is what we are trying to pursue.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF DELAY IN USING MONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Treasury Board, as Minister responsible for the Laprade Fund.
Last week, when I was in Victoriaville, I was told that although last November it was announced that the assets of the Laprade Fund were no longer frozen, there had been no grants from the Fund in the past six months.
Could the Minister give a reason for the delay and inform the House when the Government intends to start using the $87 million in the Fund to promote investment and job creation in the regions concerned?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF DELAY IN USING MONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to inform the Hon. Member that the Minister responsible for the Laprade Fund is the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, since the Fund comes under his department.
As a regional Minister, however, I welcome the opportunity to answer this question. As I said before, there are still $87.3
million in the Laprade Fund. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion has prepared criteria that have been accepted by the Treasury Board. It seems that the Department has already received about 80 applications that are now being considered, and as I said at the time, the Laprade Fund being a supplementary fund, it has been possible to accommodate a number of these applications through existing programs.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. The Minister has failed to explain the six-month delay. Could he give the House the assurance that the Laprade Fund will not, as was the case under the previous Government, be used to provide election goodies but will be spent now, to create jobs and to provide for regional development, now, and not in 1989?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member that first of all, there has been no unnecessary delay. In fact, we have been very concerned about avoiding the excesses of the previous Government and its wasteful spending, which did not go towards creating permanent jobs but jobs that disappeared after eight, ten or twelve weeks.
We want to create permanent jobs in the region and involve the region in its own economic development.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to advise Hon. Members that, unfortunately, there is only room for one final question. The Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. During his most recent visit to the German Democratic Republic, the Minister called upon East Germany to relax family reunification restrictions and to pay compensation for properties seized by the Nazis during World War II.
As the Minister will know, many eastern Europeans including Ukrainians, Poles, Czechs, Slovaks, Hungarians, Croations, Lithuanians, Latvians, Estonians and others were the victims of genocide and property liquidation in their respective countries at the hands of the Nazi regime and the Soviet Union.
Is the Minister prepared to make similar demands on the Soviet Government to relax restrictions barring family reunification and to provide compensation to Canadians for
May 20, 1987

crimes committed against them in their homelands during World War II?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have raised those questions with representatives of the Soviet Union including, most recently, when Mr. Shevardnadze was here. I want to make clear a distinction of which the Hon. Member and some other Members of the House will be aware. This Government does not recognize de jure the annexation of the Baltic States by the Soviet Union. Nonetheless, without prejudice to that legal position, we have raised the question of claims and compensation with the Soviet Union. To this stage there has been no positive reply by the Soviet Union.

speechtext: I would like to share with Hon. Members the observation that both yesterday and today we have been well under the usual number of questions we are usually able to deal with. I am considering what we can do to improve that, but I would ask Hon. Members to consider the matter between now and tomorrow and we will see if we can do a little better tomorrow. I ask for the indulgence and co-operation of Hon. Members.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the Sixth Report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PRESENTATION OFSIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Hon. Member is presenting a committee report. 1 know that all Hon. Members would want to listen carefully to her presentation.

subsubtopic: PRESENTATION OFSIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This report deals with the trade function of the Department of External Affairs.
In view of the importance of international trade to the Canadian economy and the assistance provided to exporters by the Department of External Affairs, the committee considers it
Petitions
essential that trade officers respond effectively and comprehensively to requests from the business community. The committee is concerned with the department's ad hoc approach to defining levels of service and has recommended clear definition and costing of the levels of service at each post abroad.
The committee is also concerned with the high turnover of senior managers and notes that in the last two years there have been four Deputy Ministers for international trade. This kind of rapid turnover cannot fail to interfere with accountability and sound management. The committee has recommended that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) give consideration to this practice.
The relationship between the Department of External Affairs and other departments is critical to promoting Canadian exports. Departments such as the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion can provide sectoral and technical expertise. The committee notes there have been difficulties in interdepartmental working relationships and recommends that this situation be urgently addressed.
Pursuant to Standing Order 99(2) the committee requests a comprehensive Government response to the recommendation in paragraph 13 of the report.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from hundreds, if not thousands, of Canadians in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, to point out a few of the provinces. They say that the proposal of the federal Government to seek financial self-sufficiency by 1988 for Canada Post will result in cutbacks, deterioration of service, and consequently will be at the expense of service to Canadians.
These proposed measures have already resulted in the closure of many rural post offices, the cancellation of routes in rural communities, which means a drastic reduction in service for many Canadians.
Postal rate increases affect all Canadians while basic services are not being improved. The federal Government has not enabled Canada Post Corporation to pursue revenue generating services.
The undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to instruct the Government to make improved service the highest priority of Canada Post Corporation and to abandon its policy of closing rural post offices and cancelling rural postal routes.

May 20, 1987

The House resumed from Wednesday, May 13, consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-37, an Act respecting the imposition of a charge on the export of certain softwood lumber products, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House last considered this motion the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. McDermid) had the floor.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we last examined Bill C-37 I was talking about some of the concerns that were raised in committee. I covered some of the issues at that time. However, there are still other issues which I wish to cover.
As those who have been following the debate will know we spent a considerable amount of time in committee on this Bill.
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
In fact, we spent some six weeks. We listened to a number of witnesses from across Canada who are affected by the Bill.
One of the areas of most concern raised in committee is that of certain anomalies in the Canada-United States Memorandum of Understanding. Several groups, particularly the remanufacturers, have pointed out, and rightfully so, that some of their products are not included in Appendix "B" of the Understanding and are therefore subject to the export charge on the final value added price of the product, rather than on the value of the softwood lumber content alone.
The Memorandum of Understanding specifically provides for the subsequent addition of further manufactured products to Appendix "B", with the agreement of both governments.
The Government has acted quickly under this provision in consulting with a wide range of industry representatives in developing a list of additional products for inclusion in Appendix "B".
The original list included in Appendix "B" was the result of consultation with the solicitor for the Remanufacturers' Association. It obviously was not a complete list. We all agree on that. However, it was the list presented to the negotiators by the solicitor for the Remanufacturers' Association. The solicitor's letter, containing that list, was filed at the hearing and made public.
With 20-20 hindsight vision, I guess it could be said that they could have consulted on a much wider basis; but, they took this list as the list presented from the Remanufacturers' Association, through their solicitor.
Just to follow along on this particular problem, and it is a problem, on February 13, Canadian officials asked the U.S. administration to agree to the addition of these remanufactured products to Appendix "B". Since that time the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) have continued to press for a favourable response to what we consider to be a legitimate request, one that is in full conformity with both the spirit and the letter of the Memorandum of Understanding.
The Minister for International Trade raised this issue in some detail during her meeting with U.S. trade representative Clayton Yeutter in Ottawa on April 6 last, and the Government, of course, has been continuing since that time to make all efforts to obtain accommodation for Canadian companies unfairly penalized through the lack of a positive response by the U.S. administration. However, I might say that at their latest meeting, a meeting held in Europe on other subjects, this matter was again raised by the Minister for International Trade with Mr. Yeutter, and the indications we had from the United States were positive. The negotiations are ongoing through the course of the debate on the motion for the third reading of the Bill and its eventual passage, which hopefully will come today, though that still remains to be seen.

May 20, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
The Government has also moved quickly to address, as far as possible, the concerns expressed over the fact that only 20 companies granted exclusions by the Commerce Department in the preliminary countervail decision of October 16 last are specifically excluded from the export charge as well.
In the discussions I have already mentioned, between U.S. trade representative Clayton Yeutter and the Minister for International Trade, as well as discussions between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his counterpart in the U.S., Mr. Shultz, we have asked that the list of exempted companies be expanded by including a limited number of companies that made timely requests to the U.S. Commerce Department during the countervail investigation, which companies, we believe, would have received exclusions but for want of a small amount of additional information.
We have also taken up the question of Canadian lumber . products processed from logs or lumber imported from the United States. These were all requests presented to the committee. At the end of the committee hearings the committee made requests of the Minister on certain subjects, and she has followed through on every one, and is continuing to press for the appropriate changes in the Memorandum of Understanding-and the Memorandum of Understanding allows for that type of negotiation.
I might say that arriving at an exemption for the 20 companies listed in Appendix "B" was a difficult negotiation. The Americans did not want any companies excluded. They wanted all companies to be subject to the export tax. Had all companies been excluded, there would not be quite the controversy we have today. However, because of the regional disparity question in eastern Canada, something which this Government is extremely concerned about, the inclusion of these 20 companies on Appendix "B" was pursued.
The companies that were eventually excluded account for about 92 per cent of the export lumber into the United States from the Maritime region. Because of that, we insisted that those 20 companies be included on Appendix "B", and that was agreed to in the negotiations. We insisted too that the other companies be included, but could only reach agreement on those 20.
Not all of those companies are located in eastern Canada; they are located all across Canada. But those that are located in the Maritime region account for some 92 per cent of the exports coming out of that region, and that fact was taken into consideration in arriving at that decision.
Bill C-37 provides the regulatory authority to implement changes of the nature that I have discussed, changes which the committee has requested of the Minister, as soon as they are agreed upon.
Certain groups feel that additional products or regions should be entirely exempt from the export charge, and the Maritime region is one region that has been discussed as an area that should be totally exempt.
During the original negotiations, we did in fact press for additional exclusions, not only of companies, but also of products and regions. This did not prove to be negotiable, however, and there are no signs that it would be any more negotiable now.
Industry groups have also expressed their views on a wide range of administrative issues; that is to say, how the Department of National Revenue will administer the legislation. All groups have noted the excellent co-operation received from government departments in consulting with industry to develop administrative guidelines. To my knowledge, most of the administrative concerns have been addressed to the satisfaction of both the Government and the industry. The Government intends to continue this consultative process, as the system moves along.
The net proceeds of the export charge will of course be remitted to the provinces which, it is hoped, will invest in the future of Canada by ploughing some of the money back into reforestation, silviculture, worker training, and other related areas.
I have touched on some of the important issues raised by concerned Canadians. As can be seen, the Government has been sensitive to these concerns and has moved quickly to rectify or reduce inequities where it has been able to do so. As I noted earlier, many of the anomalies, such as exclusions and listings in Appendix "B", will no doubt become less significant as provincial replacement measures come on stream.
The effect of this tax is difficult, as yet, to judge. Lumber shipments to the United States in the first quarter of this year are up 15 per cent. However, there are many factors that go into that, as those who have a greater knowledge of the industry than I will be aware-and I look across the House to my hon. friend.
I know that the strike had some effect. The strike was settled in December, and what the figures show is that February shipments were higher than January shipments, with March shipments being down. It depends, of course, on housing starts in the United States. If the current level of housing starts is maintained, we will see lumber shipments into the United States continue at a high level.
It is interesting to note that the American lumber interests felt that we had too much of the U.S. market and that this tax might curtail it somewhat. However, according to the reports, the users of lumber in the United States prefer Canadian lumber. They consider it to be far superior in quality, with far less wastage than experienced with U.S. lumber. Even with the added cost, the preference seems to be for Canadian lumber. It is considered to be a far superior product, and in many instances the builders in the U.S. are continuing to use it. I think it is a little unfair to say that this has had little effect, no effect, or a lot of effect on the particular industry shipping softwood lumber to the United States.
May 20, 1987

In all fairness, I might say that some sawmills have closed down, especially in northern Ontario. However, of the mills which have closed down I am somewhat suspect of one that closed a week after the announcement, one which has been wondering for the last two years whether to keep its doors open. The situation involving another was much the same and it closed a month later. It found this to be a very easy excuse to use to close down what was an unprofitable operation before the tax ever came in.
In conclusion, I say in all sincerity that we have had good debates on the issue. I have learned a tremendous amount about the lumber industry in the last six to seven months. I think we have given it a very good airing. We had a long debate on second reading and spent a considerable amount of time in committee. They were good meetings. We now have a Bill before us which is ready for passage. As a matter of fact, the industry is now encouraging us to get the Bill through as soon as possible.
However, if I think of the much broader scale, the softwood lumber dispute is a graphic illustration of why we need better rules governing our trade with the United States. Protectionist pressures are strong down there. The trade Bills which they are passing in Congress are frightening to a country like Canada which does not have a large domestic market to absorb its products. Thirty per cent of everything we produce in Canada is exported, and it is frightening to see some of the legislation coming out of our largest trading partner. As a matter of fact, the largest trading bloc in the world today is that of Canada and the United States.
It is our resolve in these very difficult ongoing negotiations to try to create an instrument which could handle these disputes in what we consider to be a much quicker, much less expensive, and much fairer way than is the case now. That is one very important part of the ongoing trade negotiations and that is why I feel it is critical that they succeed. However, I repeat what has been said many times right from the start. If it is not a good deal for Canada, then we do not sign the deal.
We have seen this particular action coming along in a number of commodities. Either today or in the not too distant future we will be dealing with amendments to a Bill on steel. As Canadians we should all be concerned about these actions and support negotiations where we can put into effect a comprehensive trade agreement which will allow us to maintain the markets we have and in fact enhance them.
I thank Hon. Members for the co-operation they have shown in this particular matter. As I say, I am hopeful that sometime today the Bill will receive third reading.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question.

Mr. Speaker, my question relates to one of the remarks the Parliamentary Secretary just made in terms of the corporations which are exempt in the Maritimes. The Hon. Member said that those companies which are exempt in Atlantic Canada produced 92 per cent of the softwood exported into the United States from the Maritimes area.
In passing Bill C-37, as it is now, would the Hon. Member not agree that what it really means to hundreds of small producers, many of whom appeared as witnesses before the committee, those who produce about 10 per cent of the Maritimes wood going into the U.S. market, is that the product which they have historically been shipping into the U.S. will now, in all likelihood, be milled and sold by corporations which have the exemption and that in fact the dozen or so in Atlantic Canada which have the corporate exemption will simply pick up that other part of the market because there is no way the smaller producers will be able to compete against the 15 per cent advantage of those companies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely why the Council of Forest Ministers is working right now on replacement measures to this particular Bill so that those companies, as quickly as possible, will not be affected.
As the Hon. Member knows, the Maritimes area was not an offending area according to the preliminary findings in the United States.
The Council of Forest Ministers is meeting. I believe its next meeting from which there will be a report will be in June. I cannot give the exact date, but I think it will be in early June, if I am not mistaken. It is making progress in that regard. We are hoping the replacement measures will take place as quickly as possible so that those industries will not be too adversely affected.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Parliamentary Secretary. Should the Bill pass today and become law, what bargaining equipment will there be for dealing with the U.S.-for dealing with Clayton Yeutter, the U.S. administration, the U.S. coalition, and in fact the President on this issue-in terms of remanufactured products, in terms of logs coming from American lands to be milled in Canadian mills and sent back, in terms of wholesalers who are acting as middle people for wood moving from exempt companies on its way to the United States, and in terms of all other problems which have been raised since the MOU was signed on December 30?
What is left? I believe Mike Apsey was the one who was quoted as saying that obviously the Americans will be looking for a pound of flesh every time the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) tries to use Clause 15 of Bill C-37, goes

May 20, 1987

down to the U.S. and says that she would like a particular corporate exemption, a regional exemption, a particular remanufactured product added, U.S. logs exempted, or wholesalers exempted.
On what ground can the Minister or the Government of Canada stand in getting the U.S. to agree? I have always assumed that the reason we have waited four and one half months since December 30 to come to third reading of the Bill was that the Government had some grand strategy to straighten out the terrible errors which occurred on December 30.
What can the Hon. Member, on behalf of the Government, give us on this side of the House? What about those tens of thousands of Canadian workers and companies drawn in under the 15 per cent export tax in a way which was never meant, either by the original action of the U.S. coalition, or in the October 16 preliminary determination, or in the period leading to December 30? They were sort of corralled in with B.C., Alberta, Ontario, and Quebec. What bargaining initiatives are there? How likely are we to see Clause 15 used to remedy the incredible unfairness toward so many parts of the forest sector?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, I am not privy to the ongoing negotiations, as the Hon. Member knows full well. We have some very capable people who are doing that. It is their feeling that some very positive results will be coming out of the negotiations, the discussions which have been going on over the last number of months. We have not been sitting back and waiting for things to happen. They have been happening all along. I think the Hon. Member will be pleased with the results of the negotiations which have gone on over the last period of time. They have not come to fruition for one reason. It is that the Bill has not yet been passed. That is part of the ongoing negotiating process.
Let me just say a couple of other things. I do not want to take too much issue with the Hon. Member's preamble, but there were some things in it that were very NDPish, very pointed. The Hon. Member says that a disaster happened on December 30. I cannot look at it in that way. I think a disaster would have happened had we let it go to final decision in the United States after the preliminary decision was handed down; that would really have been a different kettle of fish.
I feel that we have kept the money in Canada, we have kept the management of our resources in Canada and that is very important. That was a major reason that the negotiations took place and that the decision was made to go this route.
To say that the Bill was held up for four months as a result is a little unfair as well. We had second reading in January and into February. We had six weeks of committee hearings which went on until near the end of March. As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as any Member of this House knows, the parliamentary legislative schedule of this Government is a
heavy one. To get space for a Bill to be debated on the floor of the House is somewhat difficult.
If the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) were fair, he would also admit that I postponed third reading of this Bill a couple of times to accommodate him on his trips to his constituency, or wherever, and also to accommodate my friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who asked that the Bill not come up on certain days because he would be away from the House of Commons. There were a number of reasons that it has taken this long to get the Bill to the floor and debated. Opposition days are another reason. Let me say this to my hon. friend; now the Bill is here, we should get it through as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, third reading is always a somewhat curious time in parliamentary annals. It is the time when battles have been fought, amendments presented, won or lost, and all the heat of confrontation is over. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister, intimated, obviously in kindly contemplation of the incongruities of being a Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), it is time to take a philosophical approach to all of this. God knows, there is no point in taking a practical approach, because it does not work.
I will attempt to follow in the same vein and use third reading debate to draw some lessons from the softwood lumber case to try to examine this matter in the longer term Canadian perspective. I want to ask some serious questions about the meaning of our trade relationships with the U.S. and the rest of the world. What does it mean in terms of the fundamental issue we debate almost every day in this House, namely, the ability of this country to maintain a degree of control on decisions over our own resources and economy, and ultimately the judgment that we can expect from this Government when it comes to crucial, economic and social matters?
I am reminded when I think back to December 30 of the famous statement uttered by the Minister for International Trade upon her return from Hawaii, having had tough negotiations, that "This is a good deal for Canada". I think that statement will go down in the annals of history, along with the statement that it was a good deal when Manhattan Island was sold for 30 pieces of trinkets or beads. The Minister's statement is probably almost comparable in impact to the statement of the general manager of the Boston Red Socks who sold Babe Ruth to the Yankees because he did not think Babe Ruth could pitch any longer, and it is probably almost as significant in consequence as the contract entered into by the people of Canada with the Conservative Government in 1984. I suppose we could even elevate it to the whole question of the sacred trust.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You are still smarting.

One of my colleagues has reminded me that the statement probably even equates with that all-time
May 20, 1987

consummate deal-making which Nevil Chamberlain entered into in 1939 when he returned to England and said, "I have won the peace". Our Minister for International Trade unquestionably has a quieter place in history as having been one of the great all-time negotiators when it comes to making deals for Canada.
As we have gone through stage by stage of this Bill, second reading, committee hearings, we have seen a whole series of pratfalls, beginning with perhaps the most serious-maybe it was the beginning of the end-when the Minister and this Government summarily dismissed the consultation and involvement of the lumber industry in trying to arrive at a deal. Surely to get an understanding of trade matters it would be wise to draw upon the advice, knowledge and information of those being attacked by their American counterparts. But the Government went ahead and negotiated a deal totally and completely without any form of discussion or advice from the industry itself.
One only has to read the quotes upon quotes given to us by various representatives of industry at committee to recognize all the problems we tried to correct in the Bill; the problem of exemption in the Maritime industries, the problem faced by the remanufacturing lumber industry, the definition of what is a subsidy and the whole problem of stumpage fees. These are all the consequence of that negotiation being carried out in isolation, without participation.
The paradox is that the Government said, "We are the friends of the industry. We are the friends of the private sector". Yet when it comes to a crucial deal affecting a multibillion dollar industry, the Government cannot quite get together with the industry to work out a common approach. That was mistake number one, Mr. Speaker.
Mistake number two, which is still being recorded, and to which the Parliamentary Secretary alluded in his opening remarks a week ago, was that the Government felt it had no choice. That again has become a famous political cliche in the history of Canada, "I had no choice." The Government did have a choice when it came to dealing with the countervailing initiative by the United States. It had a choice not to knuckle under and surrender to the blackmail and intimidation of the United States and its lumber industry. The Government had the choice to pursue the matter through the U.S. trade forums and through the international trade forums. We have been told time and again that the Government's decision was made on the best advice of some unknown group of invisible advisors- not the industry because the industry said the Government should go through the trade forums-hidden somewhere in the Lester B. Pearson building, that we could not win. That shows indomitable courage and spirit; giving up before trying. If they had looked at the record they would have discovered that there was a very clear possibility of winning the battle by using already existing trade remedy measures.
I remind Members opposite that we have taken some 10 countervail cases to the GATT in the past seven or eight years and we have won seven of them. The experts to whom I spoke
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
said this case was the best we could ever have taken to the GATT. It had the best possible argument because what the United States was doing was claiming that a domestic policy, clearly initiated by legally elected governments of Canada, was unfair, as interpreted by the U.S. administration. That particular precedent, which the Americans were establishing, would have ramifications for all resource industries, not just Canada's but all other countries. That was contrary to a subsidy definition under the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade in the international trade rules.
This Government, for reasons it only attributes to its faceless advisers, refused to take that route. The Government refused to go to GATT and bring the matter before a trade panel drawn from countries not involved in the case. Instead the Government said, with an incredible sense of irony, that we have won a victory because Canada is now imposing a $600 million tax on itself. No wonder no one was out dancing in the streets with that announcement. We were putting a tax on ourselves in order to save the victory while we refused to follow other alternatives.
What is even more tragic about that is that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) said we chose that course because we did not want to acknowledge that there would be a precedent set. The Memorandum of Understanding contains a portion, written in some kind of legal language, indicating that it is without prejudice and that this will not be accepted as being a legal precedent showing that the United States has a right to tell Canada how to run its resources. However, the U.S. trade Bill that is presently being passed by the House of Representatives and debated by the Senate uses this softwood lumber countervail case and Canada's surrender to it as justification for introducing in the trade Bill new measures dealing with domestic subsidies.
Rather than winning a victory, our surrender has in fact confirmed in American eyes that we admit that we were wrong and that stumpage fees are in fact a subsidy. Now, U.S. legislators are using that as a clear rationale for writing a new trade Bill applying to all resource industries. That was some victory that was won on December 30. We have only confirmed, substantiated and underlined the American position.
One need only read the statements of Sam Gibbons, Senator Lloyd Bensten and all those distinguished American legislators who are managing the trade Bill through Congress. They are saying that the Canadians have admitted they were wrong, that Canadians have given in and, of course, the Americans were right. Therefore, we now face from the U.S. Congress a trade Bill that will have a devastating impact on all Canadian resource industries because we refused to stand up to them and because we did not use the alternatives available to us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
You mean to tell me that the Bill wouldn't have come in?

May 20, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act

Just for the sake of the record, I will repeat what the Parliamentary Secretary said. He asked if I thought the Bill would not have come in. Yes, it would have come in, but would the particular subsidy provisions that are now in the Bill have been as easily won and accepted in Congress if we had not already conceded the fact back on December 30?
We made Sam Gibbons into a great prophet of trade. We have turned Sam Gibbons and Lloyd Bensten into great wisemen in their own Congress. They are saying, "We told you so," because the Canadians have already admitted guilt on this issue. Rather than providing any antidote to the American position, we in fact have ended up endorsing it.
When the Parliamentary Secretary says on behalf of the Minister that the softwood lumber case is a clear example of why we need to negotiate a free trade deal in order to protect against this contingency, I think it can be excused if women and small children rush into their homes in fear that this is the Government that will be negotiating a free trade deal. If this is what it succeeded in achieving on the single issue of softwood lumber, then we should all be down on our knees praying to God that it does not negotiate the same way when it comes to free trade. Simply giving it all away is not negotiation. That is not skilful trade diplomacy, that is simply submission.
The fact is that we see in the softwood lumber case one of the clarion reasons why Canadians have every right to be deeply concerned about the broader negotiations. It points out that there will be a price to pay. Free trade with the Americans does not come without a price tag. It does not come cost-free.
It was mentioned today in the House of Commons during Question Period that we have seen the Government acceding to U.S. demands for open investment policies in order to get a free trade deal. We have seen the Government surrender on the Patent Act in order to get a free trade deal. We have seen the Government surrender on cultural matters in order to get a free trade deal. We are seeing the price we have to pay, and that is only the beginning of the price that will be exacted in dealing with those trade remedy laws which Senator Bensten, head of the Finance Committee, says will not be changed anyway.
We are weighing the table down with all the give-aways. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has become the Vanna White of Canada. We are in a great big quiz give-away game-turn the wheel and take what you want. I do not know who is advising the Government on trade. Maybe Monty Hall is saying, "Let's make a deal". I do not know where the Government is getting its advice from, but it sure as hell is not going the best way, from our experience, to defend Canadian trade interests against contingency action and against unfair trade initiatives, and that is to ensure that we have an effective, strong, international trade system with rules negotiated by all countries and defended by all countries, rather than back away as we have done. That should be a lesson etched deeply in the memories of Members of the House.
We do have a choice. There is an alternative to Canada-U.S. free trade, just as there was an alternative to the U.S. softwood lumber Bill. However, the Government refuses to use those alternatives and is trying to sell us a bunch of hocus-pocus about what is going on.
Sure, it hurts. The Hon. Member from Calgary is not going to like what I am saying, but he is going to sell out his oil and gas resource industry because of the precedent set by this Bill. He will be answerable to his constituents for that. Under free trade or anything else, no one wants to provide for the kind of give-aways that we are providing for in our resource industries.
Let us test this to see if it really is what I say it is. In committee, we proposed an amendment that, when voted upon, would determine the sincerity of this Government. We had before us a letter written by the Secretary of Commerce and the chief trade negotiator to Stanley Dennison, the major lobbyist for the lumber industry in the United States. In that letter, Mr. Baldrige and Mr. Yeutter said quite clearly that they wanted to confirm that any moneys acquired by the Governments of Canada as a result of this tax could not be used for certain specific functions, silviculture, recreation and the building of roads on a direct-grant basis. We raised questions about that and we asked if this did not in fact become a limitation on the sovereignty of Parliament to determine how its tax moneys would be spent.
We were debating the imposition of a major tax on a major industry and surely Parliament must retain the sovereign right to determine how that money should be allocated.
Therefore, we proposed an amendment giving the provinces the authorization to spend the money in exactly those areas where the Baldrige-Yeutter letter said they could not spend it, just to clearly outline and ensure that there was no mistake or ambiguity and that if the provinces want to spend the money on silviculture, recreation or roadbuilding through direct grants to industries, which is done in many jurisdictions, they could do so. We felt that if the Government were serious, it would accept the amendment. It would not hurt, it would only clarify the situation and clear up any ambivalence. The Government defeated that amendment. It rejected it.
What should that tell Canadians and provincial Governments? What does that tell the users of this program? First, it says that we have indeed implicitly accepted a limitation on our sovereignty and that provincial Governments are not free to spend that money in the forest industry as they see fit, but that there are limitations. There are limitations. They know if they contravene the terms then the U.S. President has the right to apply a trade penalty to Canada within 24 hours. It is part of the deal. Why? Because one singularly brilliant part of the negotiations was that we abdicate our right to further recourse to international forums. We said we would not take the softwood lumber case any further. Yet the U.S. President retained the right to use Section 301 and slap a trade penalty on this country any time he sees fit.

As my friend says, the President confirmed that in a letter he sent to Mr. Baldrige.
Let us just put this deal in perspective for a moment. We have limited our spending power. We have given up our right of redress. We have acceded to the application of an American shotgun penalty any time they see fit. What that adds up to, as we said from the day the agreement was signed on December 30, is a clear and compelling reduction in the freedom of action of Canadian Governments. Once again an unholy precedent has been established.
Let me move to another matter which is still totally unresolved. We know from very extensive committee hearings that another catch-22 in the agreement and in this Bill itself is the proposed transition from a direct tax collected by the federal Government to stumpage fee increases in the various provinces involved. We had conflicting evidence about that.
B.C. being the largest lumber exporter by far, their forest industry officials told us that we will require the Government of British Columbia to increase stumpage fees to a level equivalent to the 15 per cent tax, but this would not be a $500 million or $600 million drop in income, it would be a $800 million or $900 million drop, perhaps as high as $1 billion. You cannot apply stumpage fee increases to exports to the U.S. and not apply it to exports to Japan, or even for the domestic market. The increase will apply to all wood products.
Not only are we penalizing the lumber industry, we are penalizing the Canadian home owner who will have to pay an average of $700 or $800 more for housing. We will be applying a penalty to our export of lumber products at a time when we are getting stiff competition from the Swedes and others. In other words, we are making our lumber industry less competitive. Yet the council of Ministers is going ahead.
That also involves a curious kind of negotiation. The Government is negotiating with provincial Ministers who are under pretty clear instructions, I would think, from their Ministers of Finance to make as big a tax grab as possible. Unfortunately, those seated around that negotiating table will not include the Canadian home buyer, the lumber industry or others in the export business. Yet they will be paying the additional freight. I would suggest that kind of negotiation is fraught with incredible complications and conflict.
Another side effect, clearly admitted when we discussed it in committee, is that this will begin to have a push-pull effect on the lumber industry in other parts of Canada. British Columbia, with a very powerful and productive industry, is going to start seeking markets which would normally be supplied by sawmills in Manitoba, northern Ontario and perhaps the East Coast. Those sawmills are much smaller, perhaps a little inefficient, but they provide employment in the regions. That was pointed out several times by my colleague from Algoma and my colleague from Cochrane-Superior.

We may be able to work our way out of it, goodness knows, but I raise the same question as the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). Once the Bill is passed, what leverage do we have? It is clear that we have been caught in a conundrum; if we do not pass the Bill the Americans will not negotiate, but if we do they are going to ask for more.
1 can read to you from the statements of Mr. Dennison, the chief lobbyist for the U.S. lumber industry. He said nothing would be done until the legislation is passed. There are things that his coalition wants as well. According to him there are companies completely excluded from the tax who do not deserve to be. Some of them are just wholesalers and he wants them taken off the list. Mr. Dennison is a powerful man. He is the author of this whole business. What are we going to be faced with if he has his way?
Yes, we may be able to provide exclusion, we hope, for some companies in the Maritimes and some remanufacturing companies in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario. Once again, however, we will have to pay a price. The negotiation is not over and the ante will simply be increased to more than they received on December 30. It is another unintended consequence and another lesson we should learn about those negotiations.
I suggest we can also learn from the odyssey of stumbling throughout this process, that in the negotiations dealing with this area we will find ourselves caught up in a series of impacts, influences and consequences that are not immediately visible to the naked eye at the time the document is signed. In the days, weeks and months after the document is signed we will become aware that the price we are paying is that for which the Government had bargained.
That is why I say to Members of the House that we should pay attention to this Bill.

The day the Prime Minister initials a free trade agreement with the President of the United States we will see one of the biggest public relations extravaganzas this country has ever seen. The $12 million slush fund in the Minister's Department will be used in extensive public relations to spread the propaganda that this is a wonderful deal. However, Canadians will learn that the price they will pay is not the one on the agreement, but a price which will become apparent from its consequences.
The primary consequence of such an agreement, as we have seen in this Bill, will be the loss of power and authority of this Parliament and the provincial jurisdictions to make decisions. Our ability as a country to decide on our own economic management will be restricted. We will be giving up our ability to look after our resources, to deal with our environment and to manage our own affairs.
I hope Members of Parliament and all Canadians will consider this Bill very carefully, because there are some very profound and tragic lessons to be learned from the negotiations that led up to this legislation today. One lesson we have learned is that Canadians are in real danger of losing control of their own country.

Mr. Speaker, while I do not intend to spend all my time berating the Government, I must say that 1 find it discouraging and somewhat unusual that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) did not appear as lead-off speaker in the third reading debate on this Bill. However, perhaps we should not be too disturbed, considering that last December during the most important period of negotiations in Washington, the Minister was in Hawaii. During the final days of our committee hearings where we had important amendments that I believe the Minister, if anyone, would have understood and accepted, she found it an opportune time to be in New Zealand. Now she has found some other and more pressing place to be than here during this debate to stand up for Canada's largest industry and source of balance of trade.
The entire process in the last three years has demonstrated to me, and I believe those million Canadians who are directly and indirectly involved in Canada's largest industry, the kind of blindness and political naivety of governments when they are dealing with industries that they do not really understand.
It has been pointed out during the debate at second reading and today that a great deal of Canadian sovereignty has been given away.
In the last three years I have travelled throughout the continent to attend meetings in relation to the forest issue. I want to spend a few moments reviewing the history of how we have arrived at this stage today, in placing a 15 per cent export tax against Canadian softwood exported to the United States.
In 1983 we won the case against exactly the same kind of countervail action brought against us by the same coalition from the United States, from the U.S. southeast, from Washington, Oregon, Idaho and California. We won that case
because there was a de minimis finding. The U.S. authorities could find no injury of a countervail nature.
By the fall of 1984, a small handful of Members in the House became aware of just how serious and pressing this was when we travelled to the United States and began speaking with American legislators in both the Congress and the U.S. Senate.
Let me take a moment to quickly go through the chronology and evolution of protectionism in the United States and why we should have taken much stronger action in dealing with it back in 1984.
By July 2, 1985, we began to see the real tidal flow of protectionist legislation. The first was Bill 1088 from the House of Representatives, introduced by Mr. Weaver of Oregon. It was a proposal to impose a five-year restriction on lumber imports from Canada, to a maximum of 25 per cent of the U.S. market. Historically, we have had approximately one-third of the U.S. market.
By February 19, we had already seen the House of Representatives Bill 1139 introduced by Mr. Schulze, to impose a 20 per cent duty on all imports from countries restricting trade. That was directed against Canada.
On March 17, at the Shamrock Summit, we saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan in Quebec City, agreeing to place the highest priority to finding mutually acceptable means to reduce and eliminate existing barriers to trade. As a first step they said, "We commit ourselves to halt protectionism in cross-border trade in goods and services". Neither the Prime Minister nor the President took much action to live up to that commitment in terms of trade.
Before this legislation, which is at third reading stage today, we had a half century of absolutely unrestricted free trade in softwood and all wood products with the United States. We are the two largest trading partners in the world, and since the days of the Great Depression and Smoot-Holley, we have had absolutely unrestricted free trade in those products.
Protectionism began to accelerate and by March 21, Mr. Bonker of Washington introduced Bill 1648 to redefine "subsidy" to include stumpage. Protectionist Bills began to proliferate. On March 4, Bill HR 1950 was introduced by Guarini of New Jersey, which was later replaced by Bill HR3777, the Labour Industry Coalition on International Trade Bill containing natural resource subsidy provisions. Senate Bill S982, the Senate version of Bill 1648, was introduced by Max Baucus. On February 5, Resolution 136 was introduced by McKernan, subsequently followed by Bill 2345 which was introduced by Moore, and Bill HR2451 which was introduced by Sam Gibbons. That is the natural resource subsidy Bill which is still proceeding through the U.S. system.
As pointed out by the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), that Bill would affect not only resource pricing in terms of wood products in this country, but potash, oil and gas, as well as our aluminium industry, particularly in

Quebec and British Columbia in terms of the availability of water supply for cheap hydroelectricity. Clearly, the Americans are very interested in levelling the playing field to their advantage.
Subsequently, Senate Bill 960, the Foreign Assistance Act, was passed, and on April 24 Senate Bill 1224 was introduced by Mr. Jim McClure. That was the Senate version of a House Bill.
Finally, the Congressmen visited Vancouver on their way to Japan and attended a meeting at which I was present. We had a first-hand opportunity to hear from the United States Subcommittee on Trade and listened to the preposterous views they held in terms of the subsidy on Canadian lumber and the steps they were planning to take in an attempt to level the playing field. As I said, a small handful of us had gone down to Washington and listened to Ambassador Gotlieb and our forest industry representatives who, by then, had spent almost $10 million fighting this battle alone in Washington. We had a chance to really start to understand how quickly things were moving in the United States.
That was a window of opportunity which this House, not just the Government, should have pursued with great vigor in opening trade consuls in the United States and getting information out to U.S. consumers. U. S. consumers did not know, and probably still do not, that the cost of a home in the United States is going to go up hundreds and thousands of dollars, depending on whether it is modular or contract built to certain specifications.
The Hon. Member who just spoke pointed out that we had evidence from the lumbermen from the Province of Quebec who said that as a result of the export tax plus the flow through provisions which will be brought forward sometime in June, a house in the Province of Quebec will cost $600 more to Canadians. Times and the New York Times, in which an occasional editorial was run saying the Americans were wrong, but actually to the American consumers. That action, unfortunately, was never taken.
That one window demonstrated blindness on behalf of the Government. There simply were not any Members in the

On May 8, 1986, President Reagan wrote a letter to Bob Packwood. The President viewed him as one of the Senators who had managed to do some arm twisting with a Senator from the State of Hawaii to bring about a 10-10 tie vote to give this enormous momentum and propulsion to the free trade process which is supposed to wind up sometime next month, if it is to stay on track and get through the U.S. House next fall. The letter from President Reagan to Mr. Packwood reads as follows:
Dear Bob:
Thank you again for your forceful efforts in preserving our fast-track proposal for a Canada free trade agreement. To this end, I intend to press for an expedited resolution to this problem, independent of the comprehensive negotiations.
If this cannot be achieved through bilateral negotiations with Canada, then I will take such action as may be necessary to resolve this problem consistent with U.S. law.
