It seems that the Cabinet and the Government of Canada heard about it but did not really want to take any action to try to deal with it.
I think we have to reflect for a moment on what happened on October 16 of last year. The Minister harped about it for a few days in the press. It caused a bit of a hiatus here in the House. But the 15 per cent preliminary determination which came down from the International Trade Commission was illegal. It was absolutely wrong. It added together two different ways of computing value. It added the stumpage on one hand and the imputed value on the other hand. The maximum it could have come up with legally was a 7.5 per cent tax against Canadian softwood. That is the most it could have come up with under U.S. law. It cheated. It committed an illegal act in putting that preliminary determination out.
What does the Government do? We had two trains of action. The Minister for International Trade was going down one rail line, and out in British Columbia we had the highest level of political incompetence in terms of this whole action with the Minister of Forests for that province, Mr. Kempf- fortunately, he is now no longer there-and Premier Vander Zalm, launching what is widely known among people who

Then the B.C. Minister of Forests publicly said that the B.C. industry in that year had subsidized the industry by $150 million, that the cost to run the forest programs in British Columbia was $250 million and that the Government had only collected $100 million in revenue from stumpage. For the Minister to say that in British Columbia sent an immediate signal to the most vigorous protectionists in Washington who immediately forged ahead, pointing out that the largest producer of softwood in Canada for export to the United States-B.C. sends half of the wood exported into the United States-had admitted openly that the Government of British Columbia was subsidizing the industry.
That Minister is not in the Cabinet any longer but the political incompetence continues. Just prior to those ludicrous statements by the Minister of Forests from B.C., on September 30, we found the Minister for International Trade saying in terms of the 10 per cent dollar equivalent offer, "It is our only offer. It is done on a without prejudice basis to our legal case and it is not open to negotiation".
Sure, it was the only offer at 10 per cent. The Americans knew pretty quickly that there were going to be other offers, as we found out just a matter of days later. On April 10 the Vancouver Sun quoted the Minister as stating, "we would look like bloody fools if we kept upping the ante. It is not an unlimited pot of money". Another eight days passed and suddenly the ITA affirmed the preliminary determination of 15 per cent and the Minister for International Trade said, "I deplore today's preliminary determination which cannot be justified either under U.S. law or GATT rules". I would now like to sum up the blinks in order to keep them in perspective. While Members of the House, a very small number, were working hard in the United States with the U.S. forest people and with the protectionists, both Republicans and Democrats, trying to get the information and the disinformation out of the U.S. political system, on the Canadian side we had incredible political incompetence coming from the Premier of British Columbia, the Minister responsible for forests in that province, and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) here in Ottawa. She never really put an oar in the water to deal with this issue, something one would have expected from a Minister holding a senior portfolio such as she does.
There was an admission by the Minister for forests of a subsidy starting at $150 million. That figure is now almost all the way to $1 billion. We had the Premier saying that the deal was terrific, and so on. He said that while listening to his rocket radio in the legislative buildings. He said that a deal had been cut when it had not been cut. He gradually skated Canada's position right off the ice.
We then found ourselves going all the way into that horrible period during the last few days of December when the negotiations actually got under way. So much that should have been dealt with, once the Government had made what I believe was an incompetent, improper and naive decision to go the route it went, was not dealt with. It did not even handle those negotiations well at all.
We know of the dozens of products which I listed during the debate at report stage in terms of remanufactured products that should have been in the Memorandum of Understanding but were not, and why. We know now that the American negotiators had enormous access to knowledgeable people from the U.S. coalition who were right there camped out in rooms next to the negotiation rooms constantly feeding information in. So rather than the softwood lumber that was coming from those provinces named in the countervailing applications, those provinces being British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were dragged in, as were the maritime provinces. Dozens and dozens of corporations which had been given excluded status earlier on in July, those that had been given that status, only those 20, were put into the Memorandum of Understanding. Mr. Speaker, I think it is particularly appropriate that literally when the Government is crowing, as the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has said, we are eating crow here in the House, and specifically so with the passage of Bill C-37. In fact, it is an embarrassment, it seems to me, to Members of the House, and in particular to Members on the government side of the House, to be called upon to pass a piece of legislation which is actually going to invoke punishment on the Canadian softwood lumber industry.
At the same time as we are eating crow here in the House of Commons, we have seen the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself, in Question Period, laughing and deriding the Opposition in its attempts to get some answers on the free trade question.
Specifically, he challenged us yesterday to bring forward examples of where we have been on the losing end of the big stick of the American free trade initiative, and in fact we responded by citing the example of shakes and shingles, the example of the softwood lumber industry.
It seems to me that in imposing on ourselves a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber, we are admitting that we are in a losing position with respect to the American softwood lumber industry, and indeed on the weak end of the scale with respect to the free trade discussions with the United States.
The long-term ill effects of this legislation have been cited by members of the Opposition. In fact, it is so poorly conceived and so poorly thought out that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), after telling the country that a 10 per cent export tax was our final offer, that we would not be upping the ante in any way, shape or form, came back with a 15 per cent offer, ignoring the fact that, under a previous Liberal Government, when similar American allegations of unfair trading practices were levied against Canada, the Government of the day was prepared to take the issue and fight it out, and in fact won. We were able to prove that

Canada's softwood lumber industry was not engaging in unfair trade practices and that the stumpage fee issue was in fact a red herring.
In this instance, the Minister brought forward a hastily drawn agreement, an agreement which does not take into consideration the effect of an increase in the value of the Canadian dollar.
Since Bill C-37 was originally tabled in the House, we have seen an increase in the value of the Canadian dollar, an increase which is going to cost Canadians more in the way of export taxes.
The Government has not seen fit to take it into consideration in drafting legislation which gives up our sovereignty and tells Americans that they have that right. We saw it in respect of the Memorandum of Understanding.
I see the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) shaking his head. He will remember that he and his Party were not even aware that the Memorandum of Understanding was not included in the original piece of legislation. In the Memorandum of Understanding we see that the Government is prepared to say to the Americans that they have the right to inspect our books, that they have the right to come into our softwood lumber companies and establish exactly what is going out and what is coming in. Quite clearly softwood lumber has been sacrificed on the altar of free trade.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government are so bent on seeking an agreement that by the time any agreement is reached-and they are talking about this fall- what will we have left to offer? We gave up the National Energy Program because the Americans did not like it. We gave up the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
We heard questions in the House today indicating that Canada is being sold off piece by piece by members of the Conservative Party who are ideologically bound to the notion that somehow anything in which government is involved is intrinsically bad. That was not the position of the Liberal Government. That is why we established the Foreign Investment Review Agency in the first place.
If we look at the downside of the sale of Dome in respect of the Canadianization of the petrochemical industry, I think we will see in five years or ten years from now the ill effects of the policies and the politics of the Conservative Government. To date the Conservative Government has not turned down any foreign takeover of any Canadian company. Foreign takeovers which are not necessarily creating jobs are being approved holus-bolus, wholesale. Investment Canada might as well be entitled "Abandon Canada" for all the good it does in terms of the Canadianization of the petrochemical and other industries.
Softwood lumber is another example of the Prime Minister being prepared to bow down to the Americans because he so desperately wants and needs a free trade agreement. He desperately wants and needs that agreement so that Canadians

will forget about his other excesses, so Canadians will forget about the number of Gucci shoes he has in his closet.
We have a famous Prime Minister. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Bangkok Post on Monday, February 16. Elis legend is legion and it is travelling across the world. The article is entitled "Scandals shake Canadian Government".
Are they talking about the free trade agreement in the Bangkok Post? No, they are talking about scandals shaking the Canadian Government. I must admit that whoever wrote the article seems to assess the political situation in Canada quite accurately, because he says:
Prime Minister Brian Mulroney swept to power in 1984-
Who wrote it?

It was written by Jeff Bradley of Associated Press, and appeared in the Monday, February 16 edition of the Bangkok Post. It reads:
Prime Minister Brian Mulroney swept to power in 1984 with promises of clean government and Ronald Reagan-style conservatism.
What does that have to do with softwood lumber?

That is what it has to do with softwood lumber. It continues:
But half-way through his five-year mandate, Mulroney already is being talked about as a one-term premier.
He has been demoted as well. He is referred to as a premier. I think in the States they call him Muldoon, but in this article he is referred to as a premier. In any case, it continues:
Two new scandals grabbed headlines in Canada last week as Mulroney tried to fend off charges of influence-peddling and corruption among cabinet members and their advisers. And an opinion poll said last week that support for Mulroney's party has sunk to 23 per cent.
I could go on, but the article is available for Hon. Members. Mr. Nunziata: What is the title of the article?

"Scandals shake Canadian Government".
My point is that the Prime Minister is so desperately seeking a free trade agreement that he will do anything to bow down to the Americans, including a complete sell-out on softwood lumber.
In Bill C-37 we have the first step in a sell-out of our Canadian resource industries. We have seen it in softwood lumber. We have seen it in shakes and shingles.

The Government does not even know how to write up a Bill. It botched the thing so badly that it did not even include the Memorandum of Understanding on this self-imposed, self-flagellated 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber exports.
Time and again we have heard from a number of Members who outlined the long-term negative impacts on the lumber industry, including the potential for the loss of thousands of jobs. We have heard that a million people are directly and indirectly employed in the lumber industry in Canada.
We also know that many Canadians are hoping and dreaming that they might buy a home at some time. In fact, it is estimated that this particular tax will add about $800 to $900 to the cost of a new house in Canada. The direct effect of the Government buckling down to the Americans on the softwood lumber industry will be to increase the cost of housing in Brampton-Georgetown, among other places across the country-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

Perhaps some of his constituents do not aspire to buying homes, but they do in my community. They are concerned because $800 or $900 extra on the cost of lumber will be an added cost to real estate, which is already going up sky-high in southern Ontario and for many families bringing beyond reach the possibility of buying a home.
The most important point in the whole issue is the dangerous precedent that has been set by the Government and by the Prime Minister, the dangerous precedent which probably had its historical origins in the so-called Shamrock Summit when we all got together and watched the Prime Minister sing for his supper with the President of the United States on March 17, 1985. He said: "Mr. President, we will get you a deal. We will back off on patents, on pharmaceutical drugs, raise the prices, and the consumers will pay; let the poor pay". The pharmaceutical industry was sold down the river. The patent industry was sold down the river-

Mr. Speaker, I think this whole discussion is patently absurd. I was responding to unsolicited heckles from the government side of the House. It was suggested to me that,

because I was concerned about the precedent being set by the Government, I was somehow a Marxist-Leninist.
The Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown claims perhaps that there is not a precedent. I think Clause 6 of the Memorandum of Understanding provides a very dangerous precedent. The Government of Canada will take no action. Here we are promising the Americans on bended knee that we will take "no action" and we will take all reasonable steps to ensure that no other government Party in Canada takes any action directly or indirectly which has the effect of offsetting or reducing the export charge or replacement measures. Further, if we do not live up to our Agreement, Mr. Ronald Reagan promises in writing that "I will take action if Canada does not live up to the terms of agreement". What that means to the average lumber worker is that jobs supported by the Employment Support Act, which was introduced in 1971 to support almost 22,000 jobs, would no longer be supported by that Act because we have guaranteed we will not intervene in any other way to offset the effect of this particular tax.
In legislation being considered for passage here today we are suggesting that we make promises to the United States of America that what we do with our employment programs and our lumber industry has first to be vetted through the White House and through Washington. If we do not get the Good Housekeeping Seal of Approval from Ronald Reagan, then he can step in and revoke the Agreement at any time. If Canada does not live up to the Agreement, the President can move in immediately and invoke a 15 per cent tariff within 30 days.
Where is the fairness in GATT if Canada is imposing an export tax of 15 per cent on products only going to one country? What about the notion of a level playing field for all the countries covered under GATT? Instead, what we are seeing is another example of the Canadian Government and the Prime Minister being so wedded to Washington that they are unprepared to launch a Canadian sovereign policy in lumber which would save Canadian jobs and which would protect the ability of the Canadian Government and provincial Governments to act in our best interests when it suits Canadians. We should not have our policy on export tax dictated by Washington. It is as simple as that.
My Leader today asked the Prime Minister what he was prepared to sell out. Who is speaking for Canada, Mr. Speaker? I think it is pretty clear that my Leader's suggestion that we are moving toward a 51st state was not an unreasonable one when you examine the sequence of events over the course of this Government. We have said goodbye to the Canadianization of the petro-chemical industry, to Canadiani-zation of most of our major multinationals because FIRA has been neutered and left with absolutely no power under the rubric of so-called Investment Canada. What about our major resource industries, softwood lumber, fisheries? Perhaps steel and the petro-chemical industry will be next. We are so bound and determined to get this Agreement with the United States that we are making all kinds of sacrifices along the way.

I am responding to questions and comments, Mr. Speaker. That is what I call one parachute propping up another parachute, a Windsor parachute propping up a Hamilton parachute and they are both destined for a fall. Nonetheless, I would like to respond to the question and comment raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata).
Government Members have been casting aspersions on why I should be interested in the softwood lumber issue. I am interested not only because it is an issue of national sovereignty but also because what happens in the lumber industry portends very ill for what will happen in other industries in Canada. Being from a riding which is the most industrialized riding in Canada which depends upon the steel industry for bread and butter-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: And foreign investment.

Foreign investment? Canadian made and Canadian built steel industry is the best in the world. We do not need foreign investments. Look to the south to talk about lack of competition.
In the steel industry, we are watching what is happening very closely in the lumber industry. We are concerned that if the Canadian Government is prepared to put up the lumber industry on the chopping block, what resource based industry will be next? We are very concerned about saving Canadian jobs in the steel industry in Hamilton.

Mr. Speaker, seeing that no other Hon. Members are rising to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, I will take this opportunity to put a question to her. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the chief trade negotiator, Mr. Reisman, have indicated that a draft comprehensive agreement will likely be ready some time in the fall, notwithstanding the fact that there has not been a national debate of any significance on the subject of free trade. There was a one-day debate in the House of Commons but there was no general national cost benefit study. I would like the Hon. Member for Hamilton East to comment on the impending draft agreement and what she perceives to be the likely result of the negotiations that are taking place.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) will no doubt recall that the press and the Opposition had to apply under freedom of information for the background documentation on what was happening in free trade discussions. In fact, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), brought a whole stack of documents received through application to freedom of information, and we in the Liberal caucus thought we would finally have a chance to look at the Government's agenda for free trade discussions. Lo and behold, to our great chagrin, when we opened up this package of documents, which stood about a foot high, we found that every second page was censored because the Government does not even trust

the Parliament of Canada to deal with one of the most serious questions facing it that has been launched by the Government, the sell-out of the country.
We did not see the cost benefit analysis and we did not get the full story even in the documentation we received through freedom of information. It is quite clear that the Prime Minister wants to negotiate a cosy little deal, possibly have the House rise at the end of July and not sit until October so he can come out with trumpet and much fanfare in September or October with this terrific deal. We Canadians will be paying in consequence through lost jobs, lost sovereignty and lost integrity for many years.
We want to fight that and in order to fight it, we need to have all the facts on the table, but we are not getting the facts. The facts we are getting like the legislation before us, Bill C-37, simply show us that what is coming in free trade for Canada does not bode well for Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, my speech will devote itself to this Bill because it is a very important Bill which Canada should look at carefully. The precedent which has been set in this case is a sad and unfortunate one which the country should consider carefully. There are still many aspects of what is taking place in these negotiations that must be treated in a serious manner and not simply used for partisan purposes.
To begin, I must say that I am disappointed that while debating a Bill as important, controversial and full of ramifications for the sovereignty of the country as this one before us, we have not heard speeches from either of the Ministers who have been so vociferous in defending the Bill during Question Period, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). I must say as well that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who took his share of the defence of this indefensible set of actions, is someone, I believe, who should speak to us to explain as we wind up our consideration of this piece of legislation why it is that the surrender was made.
This is a surrender which affects a great many people. It affects people right across the country. In northern Ontario, 90 per cent of all wood cut is softwood and 6,000 people are directly employed in the industry. In British Columbia, over
40.000	people are employed in this industry. In Alberta, over
5.000	people are employed by 220 lumber companies. One would not perhaps think of Saskatchewan as a crucial contributor, but one nevertheless finds that there are over 8,500 people there directly affected by this Bill. In Manitoba, there are close to 13,000 affected by it. In Ontario itself, something like 19,500 people in total are affected and in Quebec, over
27.000	people are affected. New Brunswick employs 3,500 people in the industry, Nova Scotia employs close to 1,900 people in the industry, and even in Prince Edward Island, something like 140 people are employed in the industry. In Newfoundland, over 11,000 people are directly employed in forestry jobs.

Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
I am quite prepared to state that there was a genuine effort on the part of the Government to find a solution to the problem, but sadly, that effort went badly off the rails at many points throughout the process. As my colleague explained earlier, we ended up with an agreement that is very, very detrimental to the people of Canada.
The agreement is also detrimental to our sense of propriety. A cabinet Minister in the British Columbia provincial Government actually bargained behind the back of the federal Minister while these discussions were taking place. What is more, as Mr. Kempf has now admitted, Premier Vander Zalm himself was aware of this and had approved of it. That kind of behind the back under-cutting of our country's efforts must be recognized. Frankly, I am sure everyone in the House, including British Columbia Members and the Minister for International Trade, would join in condemning that kind of lack of solidarity at a time when serious negotiations are taking place.
After some years have gone by and we are looking back at this piece of legislation and this episode in our trade history, what will strike us most is not so much this behind the back dealing in British Columbia nor the job risks which were taken by the Government but the broader implications that cut right across the concerns of Canadians for our freedom and our future sovereignty.
I think it is necessary to read into the record yet again exactly what U.S. Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige and U.S. trade representative Clayton Yeutter say is their understanding of this export tax. They said:
The U.S. government will monitor closely the operation of this agreement to ensure that the amounts collected through the export charge or replacement measures are not returned to or otherwise used to benefit producers or exporters of Canadian softwood lumber.
How can a country possibly accept that kind of incursion on its sovereign right to shape future policy governing its forest industry? They continue:
-it is the understanding of the U.S. Government that the U.S. Government would have to approve any changes in the export charge or calculation of the value of any replacement measures. Any changes made without U.S. Government approval would be considered a violation of the Understanding.
Let us just stop and recognize what we have here. This is a statement that a foreign Government-and regardless of our friendship with the U.S. it is a foreign Government-will have an effective veto power over our future policy towards replacing this export tax. If this Parliament chooses to do something which runs counter to that U.S. understanding, the U.S. will be able to say that it is a violation of the agreement and it considers the agreement null and void. That, of course, would have terrible consequences for Canadian lumber producers. We have, therefore, succeeded in putting a very large axe over the heads of Canadian lumber producers.
This action also affects remanufacturing firms right across this country, including my own constituency. The number of
jobs has gone up and down in those companies as a direct result of what one can either consider ignorance or a direct sell-out of their interests by the Government in response to U.S. demands. As we all know, in the final stages of negotiation of this agreement many parts of the remanufacturing industry which had been excluded were suddenly included. That has to be seen, unfortunately, as one more of far too many examples of trade failure on the part of the Government. We have had trade failure with respect to the oil industry, the steel industry, the potash industry, the fish industry, indeed covering a whole range of products including shakes and shingles, raspberries, and pork, which again is of importance to my constituency. Yet this sorry record is nowhere surpassed than in the course followed with respect to softwood lumber. On the basis of their failure to speak I can only conclude that those Ministers who have the responsibility for this exercise share that sense of inadequacy and shame over the course of action which was followed in this case.
This was a case where, in 1982, American lumber companies unsuccessfully brought countervailing duty action against Canadian softwood. At that time the International Trade Commission ruled that any subsidy which might be found was so small as not to warrant tariff action. American lumber producers were not satisfied and made another effort. If at first you do not succeed, try again. Before the ITC had an opportunity to even rule on the petition, Ottawa offered a 10 per cent tax surrender on September 13. On October 16 the ITC made a preliminary ruling involving a 15 per cent duty. I hope we all know the way U.S. trade law works. It requires agreement between the ITC and the Department of Commerce with respect to damage to a given industry. On December 23, 1986, the ITC reported that lumber prices were rising, as they have continued to rise for much of the time since then, and that Canadian industry was not hurting the U.S. industry severely. That was the conclusion reached by the ITC report at that stage. That led anyone who followed the case closely to conclude that it was likely that we would win the ultimate ITC decision on whether or not there was damage being done to the U.S. industry. The Canadian lumber industry was unanimous in saying it wanted to reach that stage in trying to fight the issue. That was the stage at which it wanted to confront and at which it felt very strongly it could be successful.
Before that stage was reached, on December 30, 1986, a Memorandum of Understanding was signed which accepted the 15 per cent export tax which this Bill puts into law.
I do not know how any thinking Canadian could conclude other than that this has been a story of surrender and giving up before necessary, dare I say a Tory story of giving up before it was necessary?
It is the story of a path that should not have been followed. However, the Government followed it, took these steps, and now we are beginning to pay the price. The United States building industry was buoyant for the first period of this year
May 20, 1987

but has begun to lose some of that buoyancy. Consequently, we are beginning to see this 15 per cent tax cut into margins, cut into reinvestment hopes and therefore ultimately cut into jobs.
We must conclude that it has been a disaster but one that I hope will never be repeated in this country. I hope it will lead Canadians to draw the conclusion that the Government's trade policy is fundamentally bankrupt and unacceptable to Canadians who believe in Canada, and fundamentally unacceptable to those who care about full employment in the future.
